columns.heading: Ramps and friction
lines: FN = mg cos θ  (ramp, no other perpendicular force)

notes: ∑F means net force (the slides write Fnet).
g = 9.8 m/s² on Earth.   1 N = 1 kg·m/s².   μ has no units.   Frictionless ramp: a = g sin θ.

cover.howToUse: The left column names the slide each block comes from. While that slide is up, write each idea in your own words on the lines under its prompt. In each work box, state your positive direction, and box your final answer with units and direction.

sectionsContent.title: Newton’s Laws
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can state Newton’s three laws and use Fg = mg to find an object’s weight.

rows.title: Force · Mass and Weight
cues: Common mix-up: mass (kg) and weight (N) are different quantities.

notes.prompt: Force: definition and unit
notes.answer: A force is a push or a pull. It is a vector, with a size and a direction, measured in newtons (N).

notes.prompt: Mass vs. weight: meaning and units
notes.answer: Mass: how much matter, in kg; stays the same when you travel. Weight: the force of gravity, in N; changes when gravity changes.

notes.prompt: Weight: equation, g on Earth, and the 10 kg example
notes.answer: Fg = mg, with g = 9.8 m/s² on Earth. 10 kg: 98 N down on Earth, 16 N down on the Moon.

rows.title: Weight on Earth and the Moon

given: m = 60 kg;   Earth: g = 9.8 m/s²;   Moon: g = 1.6 m/s².     **Find:** weight in each location.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Earth: Fg = 588 N down      Moon: Fg = 96 N down
solution: Same mass. Different gravity. Different weight.

rows.title: Newton’s Three Laws
cues: Common mix-up: a moving object does not need a net force to keep moving. A moving puck keeps going with ∑F = 0.

notes.prompt: Newton’s 1st law
notes.answer: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps a constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on it.

notes.prompt: Equilibrium: condition and the two possibilities
notes.answer: Forces balance, ∑F = 0. The object stays at rest, or moves at constant speed in a straight line.

notes.prompt: Newton’s 2nd law: equation and meaning
notes.answer: ∑F = ma, so a = ∑F / m. Net force, ∑F, is the sum of all forces acting on the object. Same mass: more net force, more acceleration. Same force, twice the mass: half the acceleration.

notes.prompt: Newton’s 3rd law, and why the pair does not cancel
notes.answer: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. The pair acts on two objects, so it does not cancel on one object’s FBD.

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: State Newton’s three laws in your own words, and write the equation for weight.
selfCheck: I can tell mass (kg) from weight (N) and find weight with Fg = mg.
I can state all three laws and explain equilibrium.
rows.answer: 1st: ∑F = 0, no change in velocity. 2nd: ∑F = ma. 3rd: equal, opposite pairs. Fg = mg.

sectionsContent.title: Free-Body Diagrams
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can draw a free-body diagram and find the net force on an object, including forces at an angle.

rows.title: Free-Body Diagrams · Normal Force
cues: Common mix-up: FN does not always equal weight. That needs the level-surface conditions below.

notes.prompt: Drawing an FBD: the rules
notes.answer: Box or dot; one labeled arrow per force; longer arrow = larger force; no motion arrows; only forces on the chosen object.

notes.prompt: Common forces: Fg, FN, T
notes.answer: Fg: gravity pulls down. FN: surface pushes perpendicular. T: rope pulls along the rope.

notes.prompt: Normal force: direction, and when FN = Fg
notes.answer: Perpendicular push from the surface: up on a floor, tilted on a ramp. FN = Fg only on a level surface, no other vertical forces, no acceleration.

given: 2 kg book at rest on a table;   1.5 kg lamp at rest on a rope;   g = 9.8 m/s².
problem.find: the free-body diagram of each, and the upward force on each.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Book: FN = 19.6 N up      Lamp: T = 14.7 N up
solution: Book FBD: FN up, Fg down, equal arrows.   Lamp FBD: T up, Fg down, equal arrows.

given: crate;  30 N right;  10 N left.  Positive: right.     **Find:** ∑F and its direction; write the method first.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  ∑F = 20 N to the right
solution: Method: choose a positive direction, add forces with signs, x and y separately.

given: 40 N right (+x) and 30 N up, perpendicular.     **Find:** the size and direction of the resultant.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  ∑F = 50 N  at  θ = 36.9° above +x

given: F = 100 N pulling 30° above the horizontal.     **Find:** Fx and Fy, from the component equations.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Fx = 86.6 N horizontal, toward the pull      Fy = 50.0 N up
solution: Fx = F cos θ = 100 cos 30° = 86.6 N horizontal, toward the pull
Fy = F sin θ = 100 sin 30° = 50.0 N up

rows.title: Two Angled Forces: Tugboats
cues: Check the quadrant before reporting an angle

given: top view;  500 N at 30° above +x;  400 N at 45° above −x.  Positive: +x right, +y up the page.
problem.find: the net force on the barge and its direction.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  ∑F ≈ 554 N  at  θ ≈ 74° above +x

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Summarize how to find the net force from a free-body diagram, including a force at an angle.
selfCheck: I can draw an FBD with one labeled arrow per force.
I can add forces with signs and split an angled force into components.
rows.answer: One arrow per force; choose a positive direction. Split angled forces with Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ, add each direction with signs, then combine with √(Fx² + Fy²).

sectionsContent.title: Forces on an Incline
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can split an object’s weight into parts along and into a ramp and find the normal force.

rows.title: Gravity on a Ramp · Normal Force on an Incline
cues: Common mix-up: on a ramp FN is mg cos θ, less than the weight.

notes.prompt: Ramp axes and the weight components
notes.answer: One axis along the ramp, one perpendicular. Fg,parallel = mg sin θ down the slope; Fg,perp = mg cos θ into the surface.

notes.prompt: FN on a ramp: equation, condition, steepness
notes.answer: FN = mg cos θ (no extra perpendicular force or acceleration). Steeper ramp, less support: 15°: 0.97mg; 60°: 0.50mg.

given: m = 5 kg;   frictionless 30° ramp;   g = 9.8 m/s².     **Find:** FBD, Fg,parallel, Fg,perp, and FN.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Fg,parallel = 24.5 N down the ramp    Fg,perp = 42.4 N into the ramp    FN = 42.4 N out
solution: FBD: Fg down, FN perpendicular out of the ramp; Fg split into Fg,parallel and Fg,perp.
Fg,parallel = 49 sin 30° = 24.5 N down the ramp
Fg,perp = 49 cos 30° = 42.4 N into the ramp
FN = 42.4 N, perpendicular out of the ramp

rows.title: Incline Example: A Push Up the Ramp

given: m = 12 kg;  frictionless 25° ramp;  30 N push uphill.  Positive: downhill.     **Find:** Fg,parallel and ∑F.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Fg,parallel = 49.7 N downhill      ∑F = 19.7 N down the ramp

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Describe how to split the weight on a ramp, and how FN changes as the ramp gets steeper.
selfCheck: I can write Fg,parallel = mg sin θ and Fg,perp = mg cos θ.
I can find FN and the net force along a ramp.
rows.answer: Fg,parallel = mg sin θ, Fg,perp = mg cos θ, FN = mg cos θ. Steeper ramp: smaller FN.

sectionsContent.title: Net Force and Acceleration
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can use ∑F = ma to find acceleration, including on a ramp and in an elevator.

given: m = 4 kg;   ∑F = 12 N to the right.     **Find:** a, and 1 N in base units.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 3.0 m/s² right
solution: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². a points in the direction of ∑F.

given: m = 1500 kg;   4500 N forward;   1200 N drag (backward).   Positive: forward.     **Find:** ∑F and a.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  ∑F = 3300 N forward      a = 2.2 m/s² forward

rows.title: A Sled Pulled at an Angle
cues: FN here is less than mg

given: m = 20 kg;   60 N pull at 35° above horizontal;   ignore friction.   Positive: +x (right) and up.
problem.find: the acceleration and the normal force.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 2.46 m/s² right      FN ≈ 162 N up

given: m = 8 kg;   frictionless 20° ramp.   Positive: downhill.     **Find:** a, showing why mass cancels.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 3.35 m/s² downhill
solution: Mass cancels: a = g sin θ = 9.8 sin 20°
Without friction, a does not depend on mass.

rows.title: Elevators and Apparent Weight
cues: In an elevator, FN equals mg only when a = 0.

notes.prompt: Apparent weight: what a scale reads
notes.answer: The upward normal force, FN.

notes.prompt: Elevator equation (up positive) and the a = 0 case
notes.answer: FN − mg = ma. At rest or constant velocity, a = 0, so FN = mg.

notes.prompt: Scale reading: what changes it
notes.answer: Acceleration, not simply moving up or down.

given: m = 70 kg;   a = 2.0 m/s² upward.   Positive: up.     **Find:** the scale reading.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  FN = 826 N up

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: List the steps from a free-body diagram to an acceleration. Add how a scale reading changes in an accelerating elevator.
selfCheck: I can find a from ∑F = ma, with units and direction.
I can find a scale reading with FN − mg = ma.
rows.answer: Choose a positive direction, add the forces to get ∑F, then a = ∑F / m in the direction of ∑F. The scale reads FN; FN − mg = ma, so FN changes when a ≠ 0.

sectionsContent.title: Friction
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can tell static from kinetic friction and find friction, net force and acceleration on level ground and on a ramp.

rows.title: Static and Kinetic Friction · Comparing Coefficients

notes.prompt: Friction: definition
notes.answer: Opposes sliding, or the tendency to slide, between surfaces.

notes.prompt: Static vs. kinetic friction: equations
notes.answer: Static (not sliding): fs matches the needed force, up to fs,max = μsFN; at rest with a 20 N push, fs = 20 N opposite the push. Kinetic (sliding): fk ≈ μkFN, usually smaller.

notes.prompt: μ: units, and what a higher value means
notes.answer: No units. At the same FN, higher μk means more sliding friction (shoes on ice 0.05; knee joint 0.015).

given: m = 40 kg;   level floor;   constant velocity;   120 N horizontal push.     **Find:** FN, fk, and μk.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  FN = 392 N up     fk = 120 N opposite the push     μk ≈ 0.31
solution: Vertical balance: FN = mg = 40(9.8) = 392 N up
Constant velocity: a = 0, so fk = 120 N, opposite the push

rows.title: Static or Sliding: The 25 kg Box

given: m = 25 kg, starts at rest;   μs = 0.40;   μk = 0.30;   pushes of 90 N and 110 N.   Positive: the push direction.
problem.find: whether the box moves for each push, and the acceleration for 110 N.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  90 N: stays at rest      110 N: slides, a = 1.46 m/s² in the push direction
solution: 90 N < 98 N: static friction is 90 N. The box stays at rest.
110 N > 98 N: the box slides. fk = 0.30(245) = 73.5 N

given: m = 30 kg, sliding;   150 N rope at 30° above horizontal;   μk = 0.25.   Positive: +x (horizontal, toward the pull) and up.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  FN = 219 N up    fk = 54.75 N opposite the motion    a = 2.51 m/s² in +x
solution: FN = mg − F sin 30° = 294 − 75 = 219 N up

notes.prompt: Friction on a ramp: direction and equations
notes.answer: Up the ramp for a block sliding down. FN = mg cos θ; fs,max = μsFN; fk ≈ μkFN. Reverses if sliding reverses.

notes.prompt: Condition to start sliding down
notes.answer: mg sin θ > μsFN

rows.title: Sliding Down the Ramp: The 10 kg Block

given: m = 10 kg, at rest;  35° ramp;  μs = 0.50;  μk = 0.40.  Positive: downhill.     **Find:** if it slides, and a.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  Slides: yes      a = 2.41 m/s² downhill

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Explain how to decide whether an object at rest starts to slide, and how to find its acceleration once it does.
selfCheck: I can tell static from kinetic friction and use fs,max = μsFN.
I can find friction and acceleration on level ground and on a ramp.
rows.answer: Compare the push (or mg sin θ on a ramp) with fs,max = μsFN. If it is larger, it slides: use fk = μkFN, find ∑F, then a = ∑F / m.

sectionsContent.title: Connected Objects
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can find tension and acceleration for objects joined by cables, ropes and pulleys.

given: 20 kg streetlight at rest;   left cable 30° above horizontal;   right cable 60°;
ignore cable mass.   Positive: right and up.
problem.find: the tension in each support cable, and which carries more.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  FTL = 98.0 N    FTR ≈ 170 N    each along its cable, toward its support; the steeper cable carries more
solution: Horizontal: FTR cos 60° = FTL cos 30°, so FTL = 0.577FTR
FTR ≈ 170 N     FTL = 98.0 N, each along its cable, toward its support
The steeper cable carries more tension.

notes.prompt: Ideal string and pulley
notes.answer: Massless, taut rope that does not stretch; massless, frictionless pulley.

notes.prompt: Fixed-pulley rules and the method
notes.answer: Same tension T and same size of a for both objects. Find a from the whole system, then T from one object. Separate FBD for each object.

given: m₁ = 5 kg, m₂ = 3 kg, both hanging.   Positive: the motion (5 kg down, 3 kg up).     **Find:** a and T.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 2.45 m/s² (5 kg down, 3 kg up)      T = 36.8 N
solution: Whole system: a = 19.6 / (5 + 3) = 2.45 m/s² (5 kg down, 3 kg up)

rows.title: A Block on a Frictionless Table
cues: Hanging mass accelerates down; table block, toward the pulley

given: m₁ = 4 kg on the table;   m₂ = 2 kg hanging.   Positive: the motion.     **Find:** a and T.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 3.27 m/s² (2 kg down, 4 kg toward the pulley)      T ≈ 13.1 N
solution: Whole system: a = 19.6 / (4 + 2) = 3.27 m/s² (2 kg down, 4 kg toward the pulley)

given: m₁ = 4 kg on the table, μk = 0.20;   m₂ = 2 kg hanging.   Positive: the motion.     **Find:** fk, a, and T.
problem.answer: **Answer:**  fk = 7.84 N away from the pulley    a = 1.96 m/s² (2 kg down, 4 kg toward the pulley)    T = 15.7 N
solution: fk = μkm₁g = 0.20(4)(9.8) = 7.84 N, away from the pulley
Whole system: a = (19.6 − 7.84) / 6 = 1.96 m/s² (2 kg down, 4 kg toward the pulley)

given: m₁ = 6 kg on a frictionless 30° ramp;   m₂ = 5 kg hanging.   Positive: the motion (5 kg down, 6 kg up the ramp).
problem.answer: **Answer:**  a = 1.78 m/s² (5 kg down, 6 kg up the ramp)      T ≈ 40.1 N
solution: Hanging: 5(9.8) = 49.0 N;   along ramp: 6(9.8) sin 30° = 29.4 N
Whole system: a = (49.0 − 29.4) / (5 + 6) = 1.78 m/s² (5 kg down, 6 kg up the ramp)

rows.title: Section summary
cues: Close your notes before you write.
Use the checklist to find what still needs practice.
rows.prompt: Write the two-step method for objects joined by a rope over a pulley.
selfCheck: I can solve a cable-tension problem with ∑Fx = 0 and ∑Fy = 0.
I can find a and T for an Atwood machine and a table-and-pulley system.
rows.answer: Whole system: a = driving force / total mass. Then ∑F = ma on one object gives T.

conceptReview.title: Unit 3 / Concept Review
conceptReview.subtitle: Connect the ideas, check common mix-ups, and explain the physics in your own words.

sections.heading: Newton’s laws
paragraphs: Mass (kg) stays the same from place to place; weight, Fg = mg (N), depends on g. ∑F = 0: constant velocity.
sections.watchOut: A moving object does not need a net force to keep moving.

sections.heading: Free-body diagrams
paragraphs: One object, one labeled arrow per force. Add with signs; split an angled force into Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ.
sections.watchOut: Third-law pairs act on two objects, so they never cancel on one FBD.

sections.heading: Forces on an incline
paragraphs: Tilt the axes: Fg,parallel = mg sin θ, Fg,perp = mg cos θ. FN = mg cos θ (ramp, no other perpendicular force).
sections.watchOut: Normal force does not always equal weight. A steeper ramp gives a smaller FN.

sections.heading: Net force and acceleration
paragraphs: a = ∑F / m, in the direction of ∑F. Frictionless ramp: a = g sin θ. Elevator, up positive: FN − mg = ma.
sections.watchOut: The scale reads FN, which changes with acceleration, not with moving up or down.

sections.heading: Friction
paragraphs: Static friction matches the need, up to fs,max = μsFN. Sliding friction, fk ≈ μkFN, is usually smaller.
sections.watchOut: Find FN first. An angled pull or a ramp changes it.

sections.heading: Connected objects
paragraphs: Ideal rope: one tension T, one size of a. Find a from the whole system, then T from one object’s ∑F = ma.
sections.watchOut: Draw a separate FBD for each object.

quickRecall.q: Write the weight components for a block on a ramp.
quickRecall.a: Fg,parallel = mg sin θ; Fg,perp = mg cos θ.

quickRecall.q: Explain why a scale reads more in an elevator accelerating up.
quickRecall.a: Up positive: FN − mg = ma with a > 0, so FN > mg.
